analysis.one_liner: Restores workers' ability to sue over pay discrimination by restarting the clock every time a discriminatory paycheck is issued.
analysis.headline: Introduced with 45 Senate cosponsors and hearings in two Senate committees, the bill never reached a floor vote and died when the 110th Congress ended in January 2009.
analysis.plain_summary: In May 2007, the Supreme Court ruled in Ledbetter v. Goodyear that a worker must file a pay discrimination charge within 180 days of the company's pay decision — even if she did not learn she was underpaid until years later. This bill reversed that by declaring the discrimination happens again "each time wages, benefits, or other compensation is paid," so the filing clock restarts with every paycheck. It let workers recover up to two years of back pay before filing, covered discrimination based on sex, race, religion, national origin, age, and disability, and applied retroactively to cases pending since May 28, 2007. It was introduced in the Senate with 45 cosponsors, held hearings in two committees, and was never brought to a vote before that Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers who are paid less because of their sex, race, color, religion, national origin, age, or disability — especially people who do not learn of the discrimination until years after it began, because pay is often kept secret and underpayment compounds through each year's raises. The bill gives them the chance to sue and recover up to two years of back pay each time the discriminatory paycheck recurs.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Workers facing pay discrimination, especially women and older workers

how_it_helps.text: The clock for filing a pay discrimination charge restarts every time wages, benefits, or other compensation is paid under the discriminatory decision, so workers can sue when they find out, not 180 days after a decision they never saw.
Workers can recover back pay for up to two years before filing their charge, even where the underlying discrimination began earlier.

The fix covers not just sex discrimination under Title VII but also age discrimination under the ADEA and pay discrimination claims under the Americans with Disabilities Act and the Rehabilitation Act.

analysis.who_pays: Employers facing discrimination claims, most of all large employers with long-serving workforces, who would face suits over pay decisions they thought were long past challenge, plus the cost of back pay awards and defending older claims.

drawbacks.text: The bill applies retroactively to compensation-discrimination claims pending on or after May 28, 2007, changing the rules in the middle of existing lawsuits.
Because each paycheck counts as a new violation, employers could face claims based on pay decisions made many years earlier, when records and witnesses may no longer exist to defend against them.
Back pay recovery is capped at two years before the charge is filed, so workers learn of discrimination late recover only part of their lost wages.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core fix is well-targeted: it matches how pay discrimination actually happens — through raises and raises' absence over years, often hidden — and it caps back pay at two years, which limits how far employers' liability can reach [S3]. The strongest honest objection is the retroactive effective date, which changes the rules for cases already in court, and the fact that each paycheck restarts the clock, leaving employers exposed on decisions made long ago when witnesses and records may be gone [S3]. The two-year back pay cap and the bill's limited scope (compensation discrimination only, not firing or promotion) temper those concerns.

outcome.mechanism: The Senate's labor committee and Judiciary Committee each held a hearing but the bill never got a vote, and it died when the 110th Congress ended in January 2009; a nearly identical law passed the next Congress the following month.

narrative.text: The bill was a direct response to the Supreme Court's May 2007 Ledbetter v. Goodyear decision, which its findings said 'significantly impairs' protections against pay discrimination by unduly restricting the time to sue.
Edward Kennedy introduced it on July 20, 2007 with Arlen Specter, Hillary Clinton, Barack Obama, Olympia Snowe, and ten other senators as original cosponsors.
It drew 45 Senate cosponsors — 41 Democrats, 2 Republicans, and 2 independents.
The Senate read it twice and referred it to the Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee, which held a hearing in January 2008.
The Judiciary Committee held a second hearing in September 2008, but the bill was never reported out of committee and never came to a floor vote.
No further action was taken before the 110th Congress ended on January 3, 2009, so the bill died.
The bill would have applied retroactively to pay discrimination claims pending on or after May 28, 2007, the day before the Supreme Court decided Ledbetter.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers facing pay-discrimination suits came out ahead: the Supreme Court's short filing window stayed the law for the rest of the Congress, and a substantially similar bill only became law five months after this one died.

for.name: Edward Kennedy
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Fair Pay Restoration Act to override the Ledbetter decision and pushed for hearings.

for.name: Arlen Specter
for.what_they_did: Was an original cosponsor, giving the bill its Republican lead.

for.name: Hillary Clinton
for.what_they_did: Was an original cosponsor of the bill.

for.name: Barack Obama
for.what_they_did: Was an original cosponsor of the bill.

for.name: Olympia Snowe
for.what_they_did: Was an original cosponsor, the bill's second Republican.

against.name: 42 of 49 Senate Republicans
against.what_they_did: In April 2008, voted against cutting off debate on the House companion bill (a procedural vote that needed 60 senators), keeping pay discrimination legislation from a final vote.

against.name: U.S. Chamber of Commerce
against.what_they_did: Led employer-group opposition to reopening the statute of limitations on pay discrimination claims.

against.name: President George W. Bush
against.what_they_did: His administration signaled it would veto pay discrimination legislation, reducing the incentive to bring the bill to a vote.

sides.party_line_note: Forty-five senators cosponsored, including just 2 Republicans, and the companion bill's only Senate test failed 56-42 on a procedural vote that needed 60.

industries.industry: Large employers facing pay-discrimination claims (manufacturing, retail, and other big workforces)
industries.note: Each paycheck under a discriminatory pay decision would count as a fresh violation, extending how long an employer can be sued and allowing recovery of up to two years of back pay — precisely the exposure the Supreme Court's decision had cut off. For ordinary people, this is what makes a pay discrimination claim actually enforceable.

industries.industry: Employers of long-tenured workers who discriminate in annual raises
industries.note: Because the bill counts every paycheck as a new violation, workers could reach pay discrimination that had compounded quietly over decades, where today it is largely unreachable after the first 180 days.
